title: Working on a god-sim game
author: That1guy4226
selftext:
I started building this based on WorldBox but on a globe. Still an early prototype but Ive gotten several of the big simulations done. it can sim a population of 10,000 and has a a working wind and rain system that pushes weather systems around the planet. there is also a ocean current and tectonic sim running underneath for boats and volcanos but i havent gotten them in just yet. 

If anyone has questions or suggestions I am all ears.

comments.author: JimRaid
comments.body:
Looks awesome. What engine do you use? What is your workflow and techstack?

How much of the game code architecture are you designen or do you let AI completly loose on it?

replies.author: That1guy4226
replies.body:
Thanks! It’s Godot and mostly GDScript. 

My workflow is basically idea/design in ChatGPT  then make a detailed scoped prompt that Codex uses to work directly in the project. I then test and adapt until im satisfied and then move to the next section. I don’t let AI completely loose, although I definitely did that when I first started. I do a detailed grill me session about how I want everything before any building begins. The AI does the hands-on coding and so im more the designer/product than a traditional programmer and the AI is the implementation team.

Recently I’ve also started having the whole zipped project reviewed between larger features, which helps catch issues and bugs as they come up.

comments.author: Tung2Sahur
comments.body: Very cool concept! I think one of the hardest parts of a god sim is making the world feel alive rather than scripted. The weather, ocean currents, and tectonics already sound like a solid foundation. It'd be interesting if those systems had long-term effects on civilization growth, trade routes, and conflicts instead of just being visual simulations.

replies.author: That1guy4226
replies.body:
So currently the weather fronts move according to a global wind model, gain humidity while crossing oceans, and lose humidity over land. Rain increases the local moisture, which affects how quickly trees and plants grow. Biome and moisture also determine where farms can be built, while different terrain types affect how quickly people can travel.

The civilizations are connected to that environment too. Villagers decide what to gather based on what they or their settlement currently need. They have to physically gather food and wood before founding a camp, and settlement upgrades require actual population plus food, wood, stone, and metal stockpiles. Territory expansion also favors areas containing needed resources, usable farmland, bushes, trees, deposits, fishing access, and suitable coastlines. So placing a resource or changing an area’s conditions can already alter where a settlement grows and what it can become.

the tectonics will determine where volcanos and earth quakes are more prone to spawning. I am still working on improving everything

comments.author: tappdeez
comments.body: Wow this is awesome I’ve been exploring this route a bit but I can’t quite get it to feel emergent or interesting for long sessions — any core mechanics you’re looking to explore?

replies.author: That1guy4226
replies.body:
Thanks! Yeah, that’s probably the hardest part of this kind of game. Right now villagers gather based on real needs, settlements require actual resources and population to grow, territory expands toward useful land, and weather affects moisture and vegetation.

The next big thing I want to explore is making those systems interact more dramatically: first contact between civilizations, trade or conflict over resources, climate-driven migration, disasters and recovery, and eventually civilizations crossing oceans. I’d also like each world to build up a real history of important events, so you end up attached to what happened on that particular planet instead of just watching numbers increase forever.
